# ADR-0016: A composed halo, or an exchange, but never each operator's own width alone

> **Status:** accepted | **Date:** 2026-07-31

**References:** [ADR-0015](../adr/ADR-0015.md), [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx), [RFC-0002:C-COMPOSITION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-composition), [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec), [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo), [RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory), [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit)

## Context

[RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 3 holds each operator to a halo width sufficient "for its own neighbourhood definition".
A prototype measured what happens to a *chain* of such operators when a planner satisfies each declaration
individually — which is the obvious reading, and the one an implementation reaches first.

Three rounds of a neighbourhood operator at radius r, over four partitions, each arrangement compared against
the same chain computed with the whole cloud in one partition:

| arrangement | halo constructions | barriers | rows processed | points wrong | worst error |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| exchange between rounds, width r | 12 | 2 | 7329 | 0 | 8.3e-17 |
| one halo, width r | 4 | 0 | 7329 | **188** | 5.3e-3 |
| one halo, width 2r | 4 | 0 | 8586 | **17** | 2.2e-4 |
| one halo, width 3r | 4 | 0 | 10203 | 0 | 8.3e-17 |

The middle two rows are the finding. Supplying each operator the width it declared, over one borrowed halo,
is wrong — and wrong silently, with no operator in breach of anything. A halo point's value after the first
operator was computed from a truncated neighbourhood, so the error walks inward one width per operator and the
exact region shrinks until it no longer covers the core.

Two arrangements are exact, and the table settles what each costs in the one thing that was counted. The
composed halo processed 10203 rows against 7329 — 39% more — because a wider halo means every partition
recomputes values for points another partition owns. Exchange processed **7329 rows, exactly as many as the
forbidden arrangement**: it buys exactness at no row-count cost at all, and its entire price is the extra halo
constructions (one per operator per partition, 12 against 4 here) and the barriers between operators (2 for a
three-operator chain, since only the gaps are synchronised).

The sum is computable before anything runs, because [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 1 already requires every operator to
declare its halo width. That is what makes this a planner obligation rather than an operator one: a component
seeing one operator at a time has the information for neither arrangement.

Three limits on the evidence belong here rather than being left implied, and the third is the one that most
constrains what follows.

The measurement ran one configuration — 2000 synthetic points, four partitions, one operator repeated three
times at a single radius. Chain length was not varied, so nothing here establishes how the 39% grows with it;
and because every radius was equal, the sum and *k* times the largest declaration coincide exactly, so the
measurement does not distinguish them. Heterogeneous widths are sound by the arithmetic and were not
exercised. A later measurement of a two-pass operator did compose two unequal terms — one cell of boundary
straddle plus one cell of interpolation reach — and behaved additively, which is the closest thing to a
heterogeneous confirmation the prototype contains.

The exact rows agree to 8.3e-17 under a 1e-12 tolerance rather than bit-identically, because a partitioned run
accumulates in a different order from the single-partition reference.

**Nothing was timed, and no memory was measured.** The table counts halo constructions, barriers and rows —
not wall clock, not peak memory, not spill. The prototype is single-threaded, so a barrier is a counter rather
than an observed cost. Every argument below that turns on latency or on memory pressure is therefore
reasoning from the shape of the arrangements, not from measurement, and is marked as such where it is used.

## Decision

A dependent chain's halo is composed or exchanged, never merely per-operator. The obligations — the closed set
of arrangements, the sum, the refusal and the recording — are written in [RFC-0002:C-COMPOSITION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-composition); this ADR
records only *why*.

Why **the sum** and not the largest declaration: the widths compose. Each operator consumes a border of
validity that the previous one produced, so a chain's reach is additive even though no single operator's is.
The largest declaration is exactly the value that looks right and measures wrong.

Why **both arrangements are permitted** rather than one being fixed: both are exact, and which is cheaper
depends on the pipeline. A wide halo trades synchronisation for redundant computation; an exchange trades
redundant computation for synchronisation and for intermediate state. Fixing either would be a performance
judgement made once, in a specification, on behalf of workloads nobody has measured — and the evidence covers
one shape. What the clause fixes instead is that the choice be made deliberately and recorded, and that the
third arrangement is unavailable.

Why the third arrangement is **named** in the obligation rather than left to follow from the sum rule: it is
what an implementation does by default. Every operator declares a width, the planner satisfies each
declaration, and the result passes every check that existed before this clause. Naming it is the difference
between a rule that is followed and a rule that is discovered after a delivered figure turns out wrong along
the tile seams.

Why a **separate clause**: it binds a component that sees the whole pipeline, where [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) binds
operators and the stage assembling a batch. Putting it in [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) would have made an assessor read
a clause
about neighbourhoods to find an obligation about scheduling.

One consequence for [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 1 had to be faced rather than worked around. Its prohibition on an
operator emitting halo points, read literally, forbids the composed-halo arrangement outright — a chain needs
the halo to survive between operators. The layout [ADR-0015](../adr/ADR-0015.md) fixed — core points first — is what makes the trim after the last
operator cheap, so the composed arrangement inherits it unchanged. The rule that actually prevents
duplication is *never relabel a halo
point as a core point*, so that is what [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 1 now says, with the halo removed before any operation
depending on disjointness and before the pipeline's output.

## Consequences

### Positive

The silent failure becomes detectable, which is the whole gain: before this, an under-supplied chain produced
a plausible number and no artefact of the system disagreed with it. Both exact arrangements remain available,
so a planner chooses by measurement rather than by specification. The rule needs no new declaration surface — [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 1 already carries every width
the sum requires.

### Negative

Chains get more expensive, in one of two ways, and no arrangement avoids both. The composed halo processed 39%
more rows at three operators, and that grows with chain length; the exchange arrangement holds every
partition's intermediate output between operators, which is whole-dataset state and has to be spilled. A
pipeline that was previously fast and wrong becomes slower and right, and the slowdown is visible where the
wrongness was not — which is the shape of complaint this decision invites.

It also constrains what may be composed. An operator that cannot bound its neighbourhood — a k-nearest
operator over unknown density — contributes an unbounded term to the sum, so it cannot appear in a dependent
chain evaluated by composed halo at all. [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 3 admits such an operator alone, on the terms
that it declares its output approximate; this decision denies it a place in a chain, which is a real reduction
in what the operator set can express.

The memory ceiling is now reachable from a new direction. Nothing bounds chain length, so a long enough chain
has a composed width exceeding the partition extent, at which point [RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory) 1's independence
from total point count fails. [RFC-0002:C-COMPOSITION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-composition) 4 answers with a rejection, which means some
pipelines a user can write are pipelines the planner must refuse — and that refusal names a width rather than
an operator, which [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 2's diagnostic form does not anticipate.

And [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 1 has been weakened to make this possible. "An operator MUST NOT emit halo points" was
a rule with one clear reading; "MUST NOT relabel, and MAY carry forward only into another halo operator of the
same pipeline" is a rule with a condition, and conditions are where implementations differ. The sharper cost
is that the weakened rule is **unverified**: [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 4 checks (3) and 6 checks (5), but nothing
checks item 1's carry-forward condition. A flat prohibition was trivially checkable — no halo point in any
output — and the conditional one needs to know whether the consumer is another halo operator of the same
pipeline, which no check currently asks. That is where a reversal of this decision would actually bite.

### Neutral

[RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 3 and 4 are untouched, so no operator's own declaration changes.

A single-operator pipeline is *not* unaffected in every respect, and a later measurement showed why. A
two-pass operator — reduce ground points to a surface, then subtract that surface — composes internally: its
reach is one cell of boundary straddle plus its interpolation reach in cells, and at less than that sum it was
wrong for 26% of points against a whole-extent reference, a larger proportion than the 9% that motivated this
decision. So the additive-reach argument generalises further than this decision's scope, which **strengthens**
it, while showing that [RFC-0002:C-COMPOSITION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-composition) does not yet reach the case: its (1) gates on an operator
reading an attribute the previous one *derived*, and a second pass reads a partition-local summary keyed on
cell identity; its (3) sums widths declared in world units, and a summary reach is measured in summary cells,
which is not commensurable with them. Neither the units nor the chain definition covers it, and this decision
does not claim they do.

The decision is independent of which component performs the relational work downstream. It constrains what a
planner supplies to a chain, not what happens to the chain's disjoint output.

Reversal cost is low in the intended direction and high in the other. Adding a third permitted arrangement
later, or fixing one of the two, is a clause bump against a rule already being followed. Removing the
obligation after pipelines have been evaluated under it means every result a chain produced becomes of unknown
validity, because the arrangement recorded alongside it would no longer imply anything about its halo. That
asymmetry is why [RFC-0002:C-COMPOSITION](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-composition) 5 requires the arrangement recorded with the result — in the
evaluation configuration [RFC-0003:C-COMMIT](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-commit) 4 already mandates — rather than merely chosen.

## Alternatives Considered

### Permit exactly two arrangements — one composed halo of at least the sum of declared widths, or an exchange between operators — and require the choice to be recorded (accepted)

- **Pros:** Both arrangements measured exact: 0 points wrong against a single-partition reference, Forbids the arrangement measured wrong (188 of 2000 points at width r over three operators), which is also the one an implementation reaches by default, Needs no new declaration: [RFC-0002:C-EXEC](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-exec) 1 already requires every halo width, so the sum is computable before anything executes, Leaves the cost trade to the planner, where it can be measured, rather than fixing it in a specification from one measured shape, The segment rule leaves room for a mixed arrangement — split the chain, exchange between segments — which the arithmetic permits though no prototype exercised it
- **Cons:** Two arrangements to implement, verify and record, where one would be simpler, Excludes an unbounded-reach operator from a composed chain, reducing what the operator set can express, Introduces a rejection for chains whose composed width exceeds the memory ceiling, so some writable pipelines must be refused, Required weakening [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 1's emit prohibition from a flat rule to a conditional one, The verification needs a deliberately-wrong configuration to run, which is unusual and easy to skip

### Fix the composed halo as the only arrangement: always borrow the sum, never exchange (rejected)

- **Pros:** One arrangement to implement, verify and record, No barrier, so partitions stay independent and the executor stays simple, No whole-dataset intermediate state between operators
- **Cons:** Measured 39% more rows processed at three operators; growth in chain length was not measured, though the halo widens with every operator added, Reaches the memory ceiling sooner, since the halo width grows with the chain while the exchange arrangement's does not, Makes a performance choice in a specification on the strength of one measured configuration
- **Rejected because:** It is probably the arrangement this project would choose most of the time, which is not the same as the arrangement to mandate. The redundant work grows with chain length while the exchange arrangement's does not, so for a long chain over large partitions the ordering reverses — and the measurement covers one shape at one partition size. Fixing it would be a performance judgement disguised as a correctness rule.

### Fix halo exchange as the only arrangement: each operator gets its declared width, and the halo is re-supplied between operators (rejected)

- **Pros:** Each operator's declared width is used as declared, so [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 3 is the only width rule needed and no sum has to be computed, Processes the fewest rows of any exact arrangement, Is the arrangement halo exchange normally takes in scientific computing, which is where the technique comes from
- **Cons:** Requires a barrier per step, so partitions cannot be evaluated independently and the slowest partition gates every other, Holds every partition's intermediate output between operators — whole-dataset state, which [RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory) 1 forbids unless it is spilled through the host interface [RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory) 7 requires, Costs one halo construction per operator per partition rather than one per partition — 12 against 4 in the measured chain
- **Rejected because:** The barrier is the problem, not the cost of the halo. One per operator makes a chain's latency the sum of its slowest partitions rather than of its average, and forces whole-dataset intermediate state through the spill path at every step. For a single-machine v1 that is a worse default than redundant computation — but it is genuinely better for long chains, which is why it stays permitted rather than mandated.

### Leave [RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 3 as the only width rule: satisfy each operator's declaration, accept the divergence, and declare the chain's output approximate (rejected)

- **Pros:** No new obligation, no sum, no arrangement to record, no rejection to implement, Fastest of all: the narrow halo with no exchange processes the fewest rows and needs no barrier, Arguably already conformant, since every operator's declared width is satisfied
- **Cons:** Measured 188 of 2000 points wrong, with a worst error of 5.3e-3, at three operators, The divergence has no bound: it grows with chain length and with the ratio of boundary to interior points, which is the ratio that grows as partitions shrink, [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) 1 requires the KIND of divergence to be named, and 'the halo ran out partway through the chain' is a defect rather than a kind
- **Rejected because:** This is the status quo the measurement condemns, and disclosing it as approximation would be dishonest rather than merely lossy. [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) exists for divergences inherent to a computation — a truncated neighbourhood at a partition edge is one; a truncated neighbourhood because the planner supplied too little halo is a planner defect wearing an approximation's clothes. An unbounded error that worsens as partitions shrink is not a trade-off a user can reason about.
